title: Before You Touch Your Teeth: the checklist in carousels and stories
dek: Before You Touch Your Teeth runs as swipeable carousels and Stories on social media. This is the full checklist in one place.

body.p: Before You Touch Your Teeth is our preventive series: the questions worth asking before you commit to veneers, bonding, whitening or any other cosmetic work. On Instagram it runs as swipeable carousels and Stories, one question per slide. Here is the full checklist in one place.

ul: Is the dentist licensed in Florida? You can verify any dentist's license with the Florida Department of Health.
Will I see a preview first, such as a digital design or a mock-up on my own teeth?
How much enamel comes off, on which teeth, and why?
What does the warranty cover, for how long, and what voids it?
Who makes the veneers, and what material are they?
Is there a written treatment plan listing every procedure, visit and cost?

body.p: Most cosmetic dental work is difficult or impossible to fully undo. Asking these questions up front costs nothing and tells you a lot about how a practice works. A good dentist will be glad you asked.

Every question in this series has its own article with more detail. Tap any question in Before You Touch Your Teeth on the Editorial page to read it, and save the carousels on Instagram for your consultation.

topic: Is the dentist licensed in Florida?
title: Is the dentist licensed in Florida? Check it yourself in two minutes
dek: The Florida Department of Health runs a free online license lookup; use it to confirm any dentist's license before cosmetic work.

body.p: Before anyone touches your teeth, confirm they are licensed to practice dentistry in Florida. You do not need to take anyone's word for it. The Florida Department of Health runs a free public lookup, and it takes about two minutes.

The official tool is the Florida Department of Health's MQA Search Portal. MQA stands for Medical Quality Assurance, the division that licenses health care practitioners in the state. The Florida Board of Dentistry, which oversees dentists, dental hygienists and dental laboratories, also has a Verify a License link on its website.
Use the official .gov site, not a third-party directory or review site. Those can be out of date or incomplete.

ul: Go to the MQA Search Portal and choose License Verification.
In the Board/Council menu, select Board of Dentistry. You can also narrow the Profession field.
Enter the dentist's last name, and first name if you know it. The form also accepts a license number, city, county or zip code.
Open the result for the right person and read the details.

body.p: If you get no results, use fewer fields. The portal itself suggests this, and spelling differences and middle names often trip up searches.

ul: The name matches the dentist who will actually do your treatment, not only the practice owner.
The license is for dentistry, not a different profession.
The license status shows it is current and active.
Any discipline. The portal has a separate Discipline & Admin Actions search for practitioners.

body.p: A past disciplinary action is not automatically a deal breaker, but you should understand what it was and when. Ask about it directly. A clear explanation is a good sign. Evasion is not.

body.h: Why it matters for cosmetic work

body.p: Cosmetic treatment is often elective and irreversible. Veneers, crowns and reshaping remove tooth structure that does not grow back. You want the person doing it to be accountable to the Florida Board of Dentistry, with a record you can look up.

Licensing is the floor, not the ceiling. A license confirms someone may legally practice dentistry in Florida. It does not tell you how much cosmetic work they do. After the lookup, ask how often they place veneers, whether you can see unedited photos of their own cases, and who on the team will handle each step. Then book an in-person exam, because the right plan depends on your mouth, not a website.

topic: Will I see a preview first?
title: Will I see a preview first? You should, on your own teeth
dek: For veneers and smile design, ask for a physical mock-up on your unprepared teeth so you can judge the result before anything is removed.

body.p: You should. For veneers and other irreversible cosmetic work, a preview on your own teeth is one of the most useful steps in the process. It lets you see, feel and talk with the new shape before any enamel is removed, while saying no is still easy.

body.h: What a real preview looks like

body.p: A typical sequence goes like this. The dentist takes photos and a scan or impressions. A diagnostic wax-up, physical or digital, models the proposed tooth shapes on a copy of your teeth. That design is then transferred to your mouth in temporary tooth-colored material placed over your natural, unprepared teeth.

Published case work describes this mock-up as a physical, tentative outcome the patient can evaluate before irreversible preparation, and notes that because it is reversible, treatment can still be changed, postponed or cancelled. Some digital workflows add a second step, milled temporaries placed over untouched teeth, as a final check before preparation begins.

body.h: Why a screen is not enough

body.p: Digital smile-design images are helpful for discussion, but they are pictures. A mock-up shows how the teeth look against your lips, in daylight, when you speak and when you laugh. It also shows how they feel. Length that looks great in a photo can feel strange when you say F and V sounds.
There is a clinical benefit too. A mock-up can serve as a guide for preparation depth, helping the dentist remove only what the final design needs.

ul: Ask whether you will see a mock-up on your own teeth before preparation.
Look in natural light, not only under the dental lamp.
Smile, talk and take photos and short videos from normal distances.
Ask someone you trust for an honest opinion.
Ask what can still change: length, edges, width, shade.
Make sure you approve the design before treatment starts.

body.p: Not every case needs a full mock-up. A single bonded chip may not. But if you are changing several front teeth, and especially if enamel will be removed, ask why a preview is not part of the plan. Good cosmetic dentistry does not announce itself, and the preview is where you find out whether yours will.

sources.title: Additive Wax-Up and Diagnostic Mockup As Driving Tools for Minimally Invasive Veneer Preparations — Cureus (2022)
Porcelain Laminate Veneers: Full Digital Work Flow — Oral Health Group

title: How much enamel comes off? Ask for the number
dek: Traditional porcelain veneers usually remove a fraction of a millimeter of enamel from the front of the tooth, and that enamel does not grow back.

body.p: Usually less than a millimeter, but it is permanent. Traditional porcelain veneers require removing a thin layer of enamel from the front of the tooth, and often a little at the sides and edge. Enamel does not regrow, so the question is not whether this matters. It is how much is truly necessary for your design.

A 2018 literature review on veneer preparation reported that labial reduction for ceramic veneers is commonly about 0.4 to 0.7 millimeters. The reason for staying thin is anatomy. The same review cites measurements showing front-tooth enamel is thickest near the biting edge and thinnest near the gumline, where it may be only about 0.3 to 0.5 millimeters.
That matters because keeping the preparation within enamel is widely considered critical for a strong, durable bond. Cut through to the dentin underneath and the bond is less predictable.
The actual amount varies. Teeth that sit forward, are darkly stained or need a large change in shape may need more. Teeth that sit back, or only need added length and volume, may need very little.

Some cases can use thinner, minimal-prep or no-prep veneers. Cleveland Clinic notes these still require some enamel removal, just less, and that they are the main exception to veneers being irreversible. They are not right for every mouth, and they can look bulky on teeth that are not suited to them.
Bonding with composite resin often needs little or no enamel removal, which is why it is worth discussing first for smaller changes.

ul: Your starting tooth position. Teeth crowded forward need more reduction than teeth set back.
Color change. Covering dark staining takes more material thickness than a small shade shift.
Whether orthodontics comes first. Moving teeth into position can reduce how much needs to be removed.
The design. Previewing the final shape lets the dentist prepare only what the design requires.

body.p: Ask how much enamel will come off, in millimeters, tooth by tooth if needed. Ask whether the preparation will stay in enamel. Ask whether a mock-up or guide will be used to control the depth, and whether aligners or bonding could reduce the amount. A dentist who can answer clearly is thinking about the tooth you will have for life, not just the veneer on top of it.

sources.title: The Success of Dental Veneers According To Preparation Design and Material Type — Open Access Macedonian Journal of Medical Sciences (2018)
Veneers: What Are Dental Veneers? — Cleveland Clinic

title: What does the warranty cover? Get it in writing
dek: Cosmetic warranties vary widely; ask exactly what is covered, for how long, under what conditions, and what is excluded, and get it in writing.

body.p: It depends entirely on the practice, which is why you need to ask before treatment, not after something chips. There is no standard warranty for cosmetic dentistry. Some offices offer written coverage for veneers or crowns, some handle problems case by case, and some offer nothing formal. What matters is that you know which one you are getting.

Restorations are durable, not indestructible. The ADA's consumer site notes that porcelain veneers can chip, crack, wear or loosen over time and may need repair or replacement. Cleveland Clinic gives veneers an average lifespan of roughly 10 to 15 years with good care, and composite bonding about 3 to 10 years. Somewhere in that window, you will likely need maintenance. The warranty question is really a question about who pays and how.

ul: What is covered: veneers, crowns, bonding, whitening, or only some of them?
What events are covered: fracture, a veneer coming off, color change?
How long does coverage last, and does it decline over time?
What does it pay for: the lab fee, the dentist's time, temporaries, or all of it?
What conditions apply: regular cleanings and checkups at the practice, wearing a night guard, not using teeth as tools?
What is excluded: accidents, sports injuries, grinding, decay or gum disease, work done elsewhere?
Does it apply only at that office, or anywhere?

body.p: The conditions are where policies differ most. Many require regular hygiene visits and a night guard if you grind. Those are reasonable requests, since habits like grinding and nail biting are hard on restorations. But you should know the rules before you sign, not discover them when you make a claim.

Also ask what happens if you are unhappy with the look rather than the function. That is usually a different conversation, and a good reason to insist on a preview and written approval of the design before final bonding.

A verbal promise is hard to rely on years later. Ask for the warranty terms on paper or by email, attached to your treatment plan. A practice that is confident in its work will usually explain its policy clearly. A practice that is vague about it is giving you useful information too.

sources.title: Veneers: What Are Dental Veneers? — Cleveland Clinic
What Is Dental Bonding & What To Expect — Cleveland Clinic

title: Who makes the veneers? Ask for the lab and the material
dek: Porcelain veneers are usually made by a dental lab technician; ask which lab, where it is, and what material it uses.

body.p: Most porcelain veneers are not made by your dentist. They are made by a dental laboratory technician working from your dentist's scan or impressions and written instructions. The quality of that lab, and the communication between the lab and the dentist, shows up in every edge, shade and contour of the final result.

Once the design is agreed, the dentist prepares the teeth and sends an impression or 3D scan to a lab, where a technician makes the veneers. Cleveland Clinic notes the lab can take a few weeks, and you may wear temporary veneers in the meantime. Composite veneers and bonding are different: the dentist usually builds them directly in your mouth.

Florida has specific rules here. Under Florida Statutes section 466.021, a dentist who uses a dental lab must provide a dated, signed written prescription that includes the dentist's license number, describes each piece of work and specifies the materials. Both the dentist and the lab keep copies for four years.

The same statute requires a Florida-registered lab to disclose in writing to the prescribing dentist, at delivery, the materials used, any certificates of authenticity, and the point of origin of manufacture of each restoration, with the lab's address and contact information. In short, your dentist should know exactly where your veneers were made and from what. You can ask.

ul: Which lab makes the veneers, and where is it located?
Is the work made in a Florida-registered lab, elsewhere in the U.S., or overseas?
What material will be used, and why is it right for my case?
Does the technician see photos of my face and smile, or only a model of my teeth?
Will I have a try-in before the veneers are permanently bonded?
Can I get a copy of the material information for my records?

body.p: Two practices can describe the same procedure and deliver very different results because they work with different labs. Material choice affects strength, translucency and how natural the teeth look in daylight. Knowing the lab and the material also helps any future dentist repair or match your work. Good cosmetic dentistry does not announce itself, and it rarely comes from a lab nobody will name.

sources.title: Florida Statutes 466.021, Retention of dental laboratories by dentist — The Florida Senate
Veneers: What Are Dental Veneers? — Cleveland Clinic

topic: Is there a written treatment plan?
title: Is there a written treatment plan? Do not start without one
dek: Before cosmetic work, ask for a written plan listing each tooth, each procedure, the materials, the sequence and the alternatives you discussed.

body.p: There should be. A written treatment plan is how you know exactly what you are agreeing to: which teeth, which procedures, in what order, with what materials, and what else you could have done instead. If a cosmetic plan exists only as a conversation, ask for it on paper before anything starts.

Florida law requires every dentist to keep written dental and medical history records that justify the patient's course of treatment. The Board of Dentistry's rule on minimum record content adds that records must support the diagnosis, identify and justify the treatment, and document its course and results. When a new dentist takes over a patient in a multidentist practice, the statute presumes they have either developed a new treatment plan or agreed to continue the existing one.
Those rules govern the dentist's records. Asking for your own written copy of the plan is the patient-side version of the same discipline.

ul: Each tooth involved and what will be done to it.
The procedure for each: whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns, gum contouring or orthodontics.
The material for each restoration.
The sequence and approximate timeline, including temporaries and try-ins.
Whether a mock-up or preview is included, and when you approve the design.
How much tooth structure will be removed, and which steps are irreversible.
Alternatives discussed, including more conservative options.
Expected maintenance, likely lifespan and any warranty terms.
Any problems to treat first, such as decay or gum disease.

body.p: Fees are usually documented separately. Make sure that estimate matches the plan line by line.

Be cautious if the plan is a single line like smile makeover, if the number of teeth keeps changing without explanation, or if you feel pushed to sign the same day. Cosmetic work is rarely urgent. You should have time to read the plan, ask questions and get a second opinion.

Read it at home. Compare it to what you heard at the consultation. Ask the dentist to explain anything unclear, and request changes in writing. Then keep a copy. If you ever move, need a repair or see another dentist, that document is the map of what is in your mouth. White is a color. Natural is a design decision, and it should be written down.

sources.title: Florida Statutes 466.018, Dentist of record; patient records — The Florida Senate
